question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}+y-1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}={[0,\text{ }1]}^{T}?$

$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+y-1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-1)=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-1)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1))=\frac{1}{x+3} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1))=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x & 1 \\ \frac{1}{x+3} & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{3} & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 1 \\ \frac{1}{3} & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-\frac{1}{3} & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1)-\frac{1}{3} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -\frac{1}{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{6}.$

Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$
